name: Proxmark3 RDV4.01
firmware_note: RRG builds both the board and this firmware and ships it pre-flashed, so on an RDV4 'Iceman' is the stock firmware, not a mod. It is also the only tree that supports the RDV4-only hardware: the 256KB external SPI flash, the SIM/SAM slot and the Blue Shark BLE module.
price_note: US$355 at Red Team Tools for the standard kit; EUR329-529 at Lab401 depending on pack. Budget more: the Blue Shark battery/BLE module is US$110 (EUR99), long-range LF or HF antenna packs EUR79.99 each, and the accessory pack is US$100. A working field kit lands closer to US$500.
skill_note: Command-line only, and the client will happily let you run the wrong attack on the wrong card type all day. You need to know what protocol you are looking at before the tool helps you.
build_note: Ships flashed and with antennas already tuned. Updating is one script (./pm3-flash-all) and there is none of the memory-size roulette that plagues clones.
summary: The reference RFID research platform: an ARM microcontroller plus an FPGA that does the modulation and demodulation for both 125/134 kHz LF and 13.56 MHz HF in software. Because the radio is an FPGA rather than a fixed-function reader IC, it can talk to protocols nobody has written a driver for yet, sniff raw traffic between a card and a reader, and emulate cards at the bit level. It is the tool the published attacks are written against.
honest_take: It does not break modern cards. There is no attack on this or any other device that recovers a MIFARE DESFire EV1/EV2/EV3 AES key, a MIFARE Plus SL3 key, or an iCLASS SE / SEOS credential from the card alone - the Proxmark's own documentation states flatly that for SE/SEOS 'there is no card-only attack vectors'. Essentially every 'watch me clone this badge' video is either LF 125 kHz (unauthenticated by design, trivial) or MIFARE Classic (cryptographically broken since 2008). What you are buying is the ability to find out which of those a site is actually using, and to work with raw protocol when it is neither.
best_for: Auditing which badge technology a site actually deployed, rather than what the integrator claims
Raw protocol sniffing between an unknown card and its reader
MIFARE Classic and iCLASS Legacy key recovery
Writing and testing new RFID attacks - this is the platform published research targets
not_for: Cloning DESFire, MIFARE Plus SL3, iCLASS SE or SEOS credentials
Cloning a contactless bank card or making a payment
Anyone who wants a one-button cloner - buy an iCopy-X or a T5577 cloner gun instead
Long-range badge capture - read range is centimetres, not metres

hardware.mcu_primary_note: ARM7TDMI at 48 MHz, 512KB flash, 64KB RAM. The 512KB matters: the Iceman firmware now requires a 512KB part.

radios.note: Xilinx Spartan-II FPGA, 30k gates, 5V tolerant. Does the digital modulation/demodulation for both LF and HF. This is why the Proxmark can handle undocumented protocols: it is not a reader chip with a fixed command set, it is reconfigurable logic driving a discrete analog front end.

Discrete LF and HF analog front ends with swappable antennas. LF ~70mm read at 65V drive; HF 40-85mm at 44V with the stock antenna, up to 100-120mm with the long-range HF antenna. Exact AFE part numbers not published as a single BOM.

hardware.battery_note: No battery in the base unit - it is USB powered. The optional Blue Shark module adds a Li-Po and Bluetooth LE, which is what makes the standalone modes usable away from a laptop.
hardware.storage: 256KB external SPI flash for key dictionaries and standalone-mode dumps (RDV4 only - generic Proxmark3 boards do not have this)
notable_physical: Swappable, individually tuned LF and HF antennas
SIM/SAM slot - takes a genuine HID SAM, which is what enables 'hf iclass sam' and 'hf seos pacs'
Antenna Q-switch and a 125/134 kHz frequency switch (both new in the .01 revision)
Gold-plated FPC connector and reduced supply noise vs the original RDV4

lf_125khz_read.note: EM4100/EM410x, HID Prox, Indala, AWID, ioProx, Paradox, Viking, Keri, Nedap, FDX-B, Hitag, EM4x05/4x50/4x70 and more. None of these authenticate - the card broadcasts its ID to anything that energises it. Cloning LF is a solved, unauthenticated problem and always has been.

lf_125khz_write.note: T5577 is the universal writable blank and the client has a dedicated guide for it; EM4305/EM4x05 and Hitag also writable. 'lf hid clone', 'lf em 410x clone' etc. write a captured ID straight to a blank.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: 'lf simfsk/simask/simpsk' and per-format sim commands. Also brute-force standalone modes (LF_HIDBRUTE, LF_PROXBRUTE, LF_HIDFCBRUTE) that walk card numbers within a facility code at a reader.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443A and B, ISO15693, FeliCa, Legic, Topaz, iCLASS/PicoPass, CIPURSE, ISO7816 smartcards via the SAM slot. Reading an iCLASS SE or SEOS card gets you its identity and structure; 'hf seos pacs' and 'hf iclass sam' can extract the PACS payload but only with a genuine HID SAM module fitted in the SIM/SAM slot - the Proxmark is not breaking the crypto, it is asking HID's own security module to do the decode.

hf_1356_write.note: Writes to 'magic' Gen1a/Gen2/Gen3/Gen4 MIFARE Classic blanks, NTAG/Ultralight, T5577's HF equivalents, iCLASS/PicoPass blanks, and ISO15693 tags. Writing to a genuine locked card still requires its keys.

hf_1356_emulate.note: 'hf mf sim', 'hf 14a sim', 'hf iclass sim', 'hf 15 sim', 'hf felica sim', 'hf seos sim'. Emulation is bit-level via the FPGA, so it can present cards whose behaviour a fixed-function emulator cannot reproduce.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: The full published set: darkside, nested, staticnested, hardnested, and 'hf mf autopwn' which chains them automatically. Split of work matters: nonce capture happens on the device, but the hardnested key search is compute-bound and runs on the PC client (it is marked as available offline in the command table because it is pure computation). 'hf mf fchk' does a fast dictionary check using keys held in the RDV4's SPI flash. MIFARE Classic's CRYPTO1 has been broken since 2008; this is not a novel capability, it is table stakes.

mifare_desfire.note: THIS IS THE HONEST LINE. Full DESFire EV1/EV2/EV3 command set ('hf mfdes' - auth, chk, changekey, dump, read, write, detect) but it is authenticate-with-a-key-you-already-have. 'hf mfdes chk' is a dictionary check against default/known keys, not cryptanalysis. There is no command in the tree that recovers a DESFire AES key, because no such attack is publicly known. Against a properly keyed DESFire deployment you get the UID and the application/file structure and nothing else. The same is true of 'hf mfp' for MIFARE Plus - auth, chk, dump, rdbl, no attacks.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: 'hf ndef' reads and writes NFC Forum Type 4 NDEF on NTAG4xx and DESFire. Worth being blunt about what this column means anywhere you see it: NDEF is a data format for records the tag is configured to hand to any reader that asks. Reading NDEF off a Type 4 tag is reading a public file. It is not a security bypass and it says nothing about whether you can clone the card.

emv_read.note: READ THIS BEFORE BELIEVING ANY 'NFC EMV' COLUMN. The Proxmark has a real EMV contactless kernel ('emv pse/search/select/gpo/readrec/exec/genac/scan/roca'). From a contactless bank card you can typically get the PAN, the expiry, the application list, sometimes the cardholder name (increasingly suppressed) and on some issuers a transaction log. You CANNOT clone the card or make a payment. Every transaction requires an Application Cryptogram computed inside the chip with an issuer key that never leaves it, and the Proxmark's own notes list check-ARQC, ARPC generation, external-authenticate and issuer-script processing as 'not implemented' precisely because they need the issuer's keys. 'emv genac' asks the card to produce a cryptogram; it cannot produce one for you. The one legacy weak spot, MSD (magnetic-stripe-data) contactless mode, is being switched off across the industry. 'emv roca' checks for the ROCA RSA key-generation flaw.

iso15693.note: 'hf 15' - read, write, dump, sim, findafi (AFI brute force), plus NXP SLIX password commands (slixwritepwd, slixprivacyenable). Covers iCODE SLI/SLIX, library and inventory tags, and the ISO15693 layer that iCLASS/PicoPass sits on.

felica.note: 'hf felica' - reader, sniff, raw, dump, sim, plus auth1/auth2 and liteauth. FeliCa Lite/Lite-S authentication is implemented; FeliCa Standard's mutual authentication is not broken, so Suica-class transit cards are readable at the identity layer, not clonable.

nfc_relay.note: Standalone relay modes exist in the firmware (HF 14a relay), and 'emv smart2nfc' completes a transaction across the contact and contactless interfaces. Practical relay attacks still need two devices and a link between them; the Proxmark provides one end, not a turnkey relay rig.

standalone_untethered.note: Roughly 40 standalone modes (LF_SAMYRUN, LF_ICEHID, HF_14ASNIFF, HF_MFCSIM, HF_ICLASS_*, DANKARMULTI and more) but only one is compiled into the firmware at a time, and you need the Blue Shark module for power. Standalone captures; you still return to a PC to crack.

sd_logging.note: No SD card. 256KB of external SPI flash holds key dictionaries and standalone-mode dumps. That flash is RDV4-only.

scriptable.note: Lua and Python scripting in the client, plus a documented client command set for shelling out to.

legal.notes: Owning a Proxmark3 is legal in most countries and it is standard equipment for physical-security consultants and biohackers. Using it is where the exposure is: reading, cloning or emulating a credential you are not authorised to use is an offence in essentially every jurisdiction, usually under computer-misuse, forgery or access-device statutes, and 'I was only testing' is not a defence without a written, signed scope. Some countries additionally regulate transmitting devices generally. Check your local law.

name: Proxmark3 Easy
firmware_note: Flashing Iceman is what turns a clone into a real tool - but the repo now states it requires at least a 512KB ARM. On a 256KB board you must compile with SKIP_ flags that delete whole protocol families (dropping ISO14443a saves ~63KB, dropping all LF saves ~26KB), so you choose which half of RFID you want.
vendor: No single vendor - numerous Chinese OEMs (kkmoon, PiSwords, Radiowar, Ryscorp and unbranded)
price_note: GBP67.99 (~US$92) at KSEC pre-flashed with Iceman, 512KB confirmed - the one reputable Western reseller still stocking it. Direct from China on eBay US$47-89 plus shipping; US-based eBay sellers US$110-158, which makes no sense next to KSEC. Lab401 and Hacker Warehouse have both dropped it from their catalogues. USD figure is a GBP conversion.
skill_note: Same command line as an RDV4 with none of the safety rails: you must verify your own flash size, tune your own expectations about read range, and keep firmware and client versions in lockstep or commands silently return wrong answers.
build_note: You flash it yourself, and the bootloader is the failure point - cross-major-version upgrades are how most of these get bricked. Have a JTAG/SWD recovery path ready before you start (J-Link, Black Magic Probe, or OpenOCD on a cheap ST-Link clone); the Proxmark repo ships JTAG notes for exactly this reason.
summary: The commodity Chinese Proxmark3, descended from the RDV3 design: same AT91SAM7S ARM and Spartan-II FPGA architecture as an RDV4, with the HF antenna etched into the mainboard and the LF antenna on brass standoffs. Running the Iceman firmware it does most of what an RDV4 does at a quarter of the price. What you give up is hardware, not software.
honest_take: Hardware revision roulette is the real problem. Two boards sold as 'Proxmark3 Easy' can have different ARM parts, and the difference is not cosmetic: the Iceman repo now requires 512KB, so a 256KB board makes you compile away entire protocol families to fit. On top of that the antennas are untuned and stamped into the PCB, so read range is visibly shorter than a tuned RDV4; there is no external SPI flash, so on-device key dictionaries and several standalone modes simply do not exist; there is no SIM/SAM slot, so the HID-SAM-based 'hf seos pacs' and 'hf iclass sam' PACS extraction is off the table entirely; and there is no battery unless you buy a shield. If you are learning, or you want a beater you will not cry over, this is the right buy. If you are billing for the results, the RDV4's tuned antennas and SAM slot are what you are actually paying for.
best_for: Learning the Proxmark toolchain without risking a US$355 device
MIFARE Classic and LF 125 kHz work, which is most of what anyone actually does
A spare you can lend, lose, or brick
not_for: Anything needing the SIM/SAM slot - no HID SAM means no SEOS/iCLASS SE PACS extraction
Marginal read range situations - untuned PCB antennas cost you centimetres that sometimes matter
Buyers who will not check which ARM part is on the board before ordering

hardware.mcu_primary_note: ARM7TDMI at 48 MHz. CRITICAL: many units ship the AT91SAM7S256 (256KB) instead as a cost saving. Read the part marking on the chip, or the size reported in the client's start-up banner. The Iceman repo requires 512KB for a full build.

radios.note: Xilinx Spartan-II FPGA, same architecture as the RDV4 - the silicon is not where these boards are cheap.
HF antenna etched directly into the mainboard PCB, LF antenna a bare coil on brass standoffs. Neither is tuned per unit, which is where the read-range deficit against an RDV4 comes from.

hardware.battery_note: No battery. An optional stacking battery shield (typically 600mAh Li-Po) is sold separately and is what makes standalone modes usable.
hardware.storage: None - no external SPI flash. On-device key dictionaries and flash-backed standalone dumps are RDV4-only features.
hardware.case: Usually sold bare-board or with a thin acrylic sandwich
notable_physical: Detachable LF antenna on brass standoffs
HF antenna integrated into the mainboard
No SIM/SAM slot
Original Chinese units enumerate as USB VID 2D2D PID 504D; official builds use 9AC4/4B8F

lf_125khz_read.note: Same firmware support as an RDV4 (EM410x, HID Prox, Indala, AWID, ioProx, Hitag, FDX-B and the rest), but the untuned coil gives noticeably shorter range. Fine on contact, less forgiving through a wallet.

lf_125khz_write.note: T5577 and EM4305 writing works identically - this is firmware, not antenna dependent, as long as you can hold the blank against the coil.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: Full sim and brute-force command set, but standalone brute-force modes need the add-on battery shield to be useful at a door.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443A/B, ISO15693, iCLASS/PicoPass, FeliCa, Legic all supported in firmware. The PCB-etched HF antenna is the limit, not the code. No SIM/SAM slot means the HID-SAM path to iCLASS SE / SEOS PACS extraction is unavailable on this hardware regardless of firmware.

hf_1356_write.note: Magic MIFARE Classic blanks, NTAG/Ultralight, iCLASS/PicoPass and ISO15693 writing all work.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Bit-level FPGA emulation, same as RDV4.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: darkside, nested, staticnested, hardnested and autopwn all available. One practical loss: 'hf mf fchk' fast dictionary checking pulls keys from the RDV4's SPI flash, which this board does not have, so large dictionary runs go over USB from the client instead.

mifare_desfire.note: Identical to the RDV4: full command set, authenticate-with-known-key only, dictionary check only. No DESFire AES key recovery exists on any hardware.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: Type 4 NDEF read/write on NTAG4xx and DESFire. A data-format capability, not a security bypass.

emv_read.note: The same EMV kernel as the RDV4. Gets PAN, expiry and sometimes a transaction log off a contactless bank card. Cannot clone the card or make a payment - the cryptogram is generated inside the chip with an issuer key. See the RDV4 entry for the full explanation.

felica.note: Reader, sniff, dump, sim, Lite/Lite-S auth. FeliCa Standard crypto is not broken.

standalone_untethered.note: The modes are in the firmware but need the add-on battery shield, and any mode that expects external SPI flash will not build for this board.

sd_logging.note: Notable absence. No SD card and no external SPI flash, unlike the RDV4.

scriptable.note: Lua and Python via the client, identical to the RDV4.

legal.notes: Same position as any Proxmark3: owning one is legal in most countries, using it against credentials you are not authorised to use is not. Ordering direct from China means a customs declaration that says something vague; that is a customs question, not evidence of anything, but it is worth knowing which country you are importing into. Check your local law.

name: Proxmark3 Easy
firmware_note: Whatever the seller flashed before shipping: usually an old fork of the upstream Proxmark client, sometimes wrapped in a Chinese-language GUI. Treat it as something to overwrite on day one, not as a product.
vendor: No single vendor - numerous Chinese OEMs (kkmoon, PiSwords, Radiowar, Ryscorp and unbranded)
price_note: Same hardware and price as the Iceman-flashed entry - the difference is only which firmware is on it when it arrives. Sellers who pre-flash Iceman (KSEC does) are worth the premium over a bare eBay unit.
skill_note: Not because the stock firmware is powerful, but because diagnosing it is: when firmware and client versions do not match, commands do not error, they return wrong readings. You need enough experience to recognise a plausible-looking wrong answer.
build_note: The only sensible first move is to reflash it with Iceman. Do that before you form any opinion about what the hardware can do.
summary: The same Proxmark3 Easy board as it arrives from the seller, running whatever firmware and client the OEM bundled. Listed separately because a meaningful number of buyers never reflash, and then judge the Proxmark platform on this.
honest_take: This is the single most common reason people conclude 'my Proxmark is broken'. The bundled firmware and the bundled client are frequently from different versions, and a version mismatch on a Proxmark does not throw an error - it silently returns garbage that looks like data. Add a GUI wrapper that is often Chinese-only and undocumented, and you have a device that appears to work while giving you wrong answers. There is no upside to keeping it: the stock build has no attack the Iceman build lacks. Flash it, then evaluate it.
best_for: Nothing - this configuration exists to be replaced
not_for: Any result you intend to rely on
Learning the platform - you will be learning a fork that does not match any current documentation

name: Chameleon Ultra
firmware_note: GPL-3.0, actively developed. v2.2.0 (July 2026) added ioProx, EM4x05/EM4x69, IDTECK and Jablotron LF support, raw field capture ('lf sniff', 'hf 14a sniff'), Flipper .nfc file import, and an 'hf mf autopwn' with integrated HardNested in the CLI.
price_note: US$130 at Hacker Warehouse; EUR129 at Lab401; GBP109.99 (~US$149) at KSEC. A cut-down 'Chameleon Lite' sells for EUR59 - same emulation, but it omits the MFRC522 so it cannot read or write HF tags at all, only simulate them. Buy the Lite only if you already have a Proxmark to do the reading.
skill_note: The mobile app makes basic clone-and-emulate genuinely easy, but interpreting what a failed emulation means still requires knowing which card technology you are up against.
build_note: Works out of the box over BLE from the MTools app; firmware updates are DFU packages over USB-C or BLE.
summary: A keychain-sized dual-frequency card emulator: 8 LF slots and 8 HF slots, switched with two buttons, running about six months on a 90mAh cell. HF emulation runs on the nRF52840's on-die NFC-A tag peripheral, which draws around 5mA and does not need the CPU awake - this is why it behaves like a real card rather than like a microcontroller pretending to be one. A separate MFRC522 gives it reader capability so it can capture a card as well as replay it.
honest_take: Two hard limits get papered over in the marketing. First, the reader front end is an MFRC522, which is ISO14443A-only silicon: no ISO15693, no ISO14443B, no FeliCa, ever, at any firmware version. That rules out iCODE, most library and ski-pass tags, and the HF layer iCLASS rides on. Second, seeing 'DESFire EV1 & EV2' and 'MIFARE Plus' in the supported-tag list means it can hold a conversation in those protocols at 106 kbit/s - not that it can clone one. Without the site's AES keys a real DESFire reader will reject the emulation instantly, and the firmware's own whitepaper flags DESFire as low-bit-rate only. Where it genuinely beats a Flipper Zero is emulation fidelity: full control of UID, SAK, ATQA and ATS, and a detection mode that logs reader nonces for MFKEY32 recovery while sitting in the field.

Anyone who wants Proxmark-grade emulation without carrying a Proxmark
not_for: ISO15693 / NFC-V, ISO14443B or FeliCa - the RC522 physically cannot
iCLASS, iCLASS SE or SEOS
Cloning a DESFire or a bank card
Sniffing a full reader-card exchange - the raw capture added in v2.2.0 is field capture, not a decoded protocol trace like a Proxmark's

hardware.mcu_primary_note: ARM Cortex-M4F at 64 MHz, 1MB flash, 256KB RAM, BLE 5.0 and USB 2.0. Its on-die NFC-A tag peripheral does HF card emulation autonomously at ~5mA/3.3V without waking the CPU, which is where the six-month battery figure comes from.

radios.note: 13.56 MHz ISO14443A card emulation. Passive-field capable, so it presents like a real card.
13.56 MHz reader/writer. ISO14443A-only silicon - this single chip choice is why ISO15693, ISO14443B and FeliCa are permanently out of scope. The Chameleon Lite omits this chip entirely.
125 kHz LF read/write/emulate on a second antenna PCB, driven from the nRF52840 with discrete analog. The vendor does not publish a part number for the LF front end and none could be confirmed.

hardware.battery_note: Li-Po. The ~6 month figure is idle/standby with occasional use, and holds up in independent reviews because emulation runs on the NFC peripheral rather than the CPU.
hardware.storage: Internal flash organised as 8 HF card slots and 8 LF card slots
hardware.case: Plastic, two-PCB sandwich with a spacer
notable_physical: Two buttons (A/B) for slot switching with no host needed
8 slot-indicator LEDs
HF antenna on the mainboard, LF antenna on a second board - the reason it is a sandwich

lf_125khz_read.note: EM410x, T5577, HID Prox, Indala, FDX-B, Paradox, AWID, PAC/Stanley, Viking, Keri, Securakey, Gallagher, and (added in v2.2.0) ioProx, EM4x05/EM4x69, IDTECK PSK1 and Jablotron. All of these are unauthenticated by design - the card shouts its ID at anything that powers it.

lf_125khz_write.note: Writes captured IDs to T5577 blanks. The vendor's own docs note that for many of the exotic LF formats the hardware and codec are ready but the application layer is not implemented, so read-and-emulate works where write-to-blank may not.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: 8 LF slots. EM410x (ASK) and HID Prox (FSK) are fully implemented at the application layer; 15+ further formats have codec support with partial or absent application-layer handling.

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443A only, via the MFRC522: MIFARE Classic 1K/2K/4K (4- and 7-byte UID), Ultralight/C/EV1, NTAG 210-218, and DESFire/EV1/EV2 at low bit rate. Not a limitation of firmware - the RC522 does not implement anything else.

hf_1356_write.note: Writes MIFARE Classic data to 'magic' Gen1a/Gen2 blanks and supports magic UID/SAK modes. It is not a general-purpose HF writer.

hf_1356_emulate.note: 8 HF slots with full control of UID, SAK, ATQA and ATS, plus a configurable PRNG for MF1 emulation (added v2.2.0). This is the device's genuine strength and it is measurably better than a Flipper Zero at convincing a real reader.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: MFKEY32 v2, Darkside, Nested, StaticNested and HardNested. Split of work: the device does the capture - detection mode logs reader nonces while it sits in the field emulating - and the key computation runs in the client, either the Python CLI on a PC or the MTools mobile app over BLE. v2.2.0 added an 'hf mf autopwn' that chains the whole sequence including HardNested.

mifare_desfire.note: Read this carefully. DESFire EV1/EV2 appear in every reseller's supported-tag list, and what that means is that the device can exchange ISO14443A frames with one at 106 kbit/s (the whitepaper states higher bit rates are hardware-limited). It cannot recover a DESFire AES key - nothing can - so it cannot clone a keyed DESFire credential. Emulating a DESFire shape without the keys gets rejected by any real reader.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: Emulates NTAG21x and Ultralight (NFC Forum Type 2) well, and can present DESFire-shaped Type 4 structures at low bit rate. summary: The original credit-card-form-factor NFC emulator from the academic group at Ruhr University Bochum, productised by Kasper & Oswald after a 1,700-backer Kickstarter. An ATxmega128A4U clocked at 27.12 MHz - exactly twice 13.56 MHz - driving a single HF antenna, with 8 slots of card configurations. It emulates, it sniffs, and it barely reads.
honest_take: It is 13.56 MHz only. The project's own support table lists 'any non-13.56 MHz tag' as NO at the hardware, software and application layers, so there is no LF 125 kHz path at all - no HID Prox, no EM4100. That single fact makes it the wrong tool for most physical access work, where LF is still enormously common. Reader mode is also far weaker than people expect: there is still no implemented command to read a MIFARE Classic or a DESFire, only 'dump_mfu' for Ultralight, even though the crypto primitives are sitting in the firmware. What it uniquely does, and the Chameleon Ultra cannot, is emulate and sniff ISO15693. Its DESFire emulation is also the most serious in this batch - real AES ciphers, app and key creation, encrypted file operations - but note that this is emulating a DESFire whose keys you supply, not breaking anyone's. EV2/EV3-specific functionality is explicitly absent. Development has been quiet since August 2023.

summary: A Proxmark3-derived RF platform bolted to a Linux single-board computer with a 1.3-inch screen, buttons and a 2000mAh battery, wrapped in a clone-this-badge wizard. The genuinely useful part is that the Linux side runs the Proxmark client on the device itself, so MIFARE Classic key recovery finishes in your hand instead of on a laptop.
honest_take: You are paying roughly three Proxmark3s for a screen and a wizard, and the wizard automates the half of the problem that was already easy. LF 125 kHz cloning is unauthenticated by design and MIFARE Classic has been broken since 2008; those are what the one-button flow handles. Lab401's own spec sheet lists MIFARE DESFire, iCLASS Elite with custom keys, and EMV as NOT supported. The 'iCLASS SE / SEOS cloning' headline is the one to read carefully: it needs the separate EUR425 iCS Decoder, and what it performs is a downgrade attack, not a clone. The decoder extracts the PACS payload from the secure credential, and the iCopy-X writes those Wiegand bits onto a legacy iCLASS/PicoPass or T5577 blank. That blank only opens the door if the reader still has legacy iCLASS or ProxII formats enabled - if the site turned legacy off, you have an expensive coaster. The Proxmark project's own downgrade notes state there are no card-only attack vectors against SE/SEOS. Finally, the price tiers are a software paywall on identical hardware, and there is a free open-source firmware that removes them entirely.

summary: A card-sized board pairing a SAMD21 Cortex-M0+ with an NXP PN7150 NFC controller, sold as a contactless skimmer detector. honest_take: The headline feature is an LED that lights when something nearby is energising a 13.56 MHz field. That is a real and occasionally useful primitive, but it is not skimmer detection in any meaningful sense: a legitimate payment terminal, a door reader and a hostile skimmer all produce an identical RF field, and the shipped firmware does no signature matching, no protocol fingerprinting and no reader identification. It tells you a reader is on, nothing about whose it is. The interesting hardware is the PN7150, and to use it you have to write your own firmware, which is a different product from the one being sold. Electronic Cats have retired it - it is gone from their store, sold out on Tindie since January 2023, and they now point buyers at the BomberCat (US$119), which folds the same reader-detection into a device that also does NFC relay and magstripe work. Do not confuse this with the plain 'Hunter Cat', a separate and still-current US$41-46 magnetic-stripe skimmer detector.

hardware.mcu_primary_note: ARM Cortex-M0+. Provides the USB interface and drives the NFC controller. Exact SAMD21 variant not specified by the vendor.

radios.note: NXP full-NFC controller with an integrated firmware stack: ISO14443A, ISO14443B, NFCIP-1/2, FeliCa PCD mode, NFC Forum tag types 1-5, and MIFARE Classic crypto. Supports reader/writer, card emulation and peer-to-peer modes. All the capability in this device comes from this chip.

hardware.battery_note: Ships with a battery; capacity not published.

detect_skimmer.note: SAY WHAT IT MATCHES ON: nothing. It detects the presence of an active 13.56 MHz reader field and flashes a red LED. There is no signature list, no MAC or UID matching, no protocol fingerprinting and no way to tell a hostile reader from a shop's payment terminal or a building's door reader. Treat it as an RF-field presence indicator, which is what it is.

hf_1356_read.note: The PN7150 is a capable reader (ISO14443A/B, FeliCa, NFC Forum T1-T5) but the shipped firmware is a detector. Reader functionality means writing your own Arduino or CircuitPython code.

hf_1356_emulate.note: PN7150 card-emulation mode is available in hardware; shipped firmware does not expose it.

lf_125khz_read.note: Notable absence. 13.56 MHz only. It cannot see an HID Prox or EM4100 badge at all.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: PN7150 handles NFC Forum tag types 1 through 5 including Type 4 NDEF. Reachable through your own firmware, not through the shipped detector build.

iso15693.note: PN7150 supports NFC Forum Type 5 (ISO15693). Resellers list it. No shipped-firmware application uses it.

felica.note: PN7150 has FeliCa PCD mode. Again, hardware capability with no shipped application.

emv_read.note: No EMV kernel. The PN7150 will happily carry ISO14443-4 APDUs, so someone could write EMV support, but nothing ships. And even a complete EMV read would only give PAN and expiry - never the ability to clone the card or make a payment, because the transaction cryptogram is generated inside the chip with an issuer key.

scriptable.note: Arduino and CircuitPython compatible with a UF2 bootloader. This is genuinely the device's best feature and the reason to want one.

standalone_untethered.note: Battery powered with LED output - it works in a pocket with nothing attached.

legal.notes: A passive field detector with no transmit function in its shipped configuration - unremarkable to own or carry anywhere. If you reflash it as a reader or an emulator, the legal position becomes that of any NFC reader: reading or emulating credentials you are not authorised to use is an offence in most jurisdictions. Check your local law.

name: ACR122U
firmware_note: Closed vendor firmware on an ST7 MCU that presents the PN532 to the host as a USB CCID smartcard reader. That wrapper is why the device works everywhere through PC/SC and why libnfc has to reach the PN532 through a CCID escape command.
price_note: US$28.88-49.99 on Amazon, clustering around US$32-38. But read the status field: ACS has end-of-lifed the genuine article and states on its own product page that there have been 'widespread reports of counterfeit or non-genuine ACR122U units on the market'. Whatever arrives at this price is almost certainly a clone. ACS's named replacement is the ACR1552U at US$65.95. Neither Lab401 nor KSEC stocks an ACR122U at all.
skill_note: The reader is trivial; the toolchain is not. Getting libnfc, pcscd and the CCID driver to cooperate on Linux - and stop fighting each other over the device - is the actual difficulty, and it is where most people give up.
build_note: Plug in and install drivers. On Linux you will likely need to blacklist a kernel module and configure PCSC before libnfc sees it.
summary: The ubiquitous cheap USB NFC reader: an NXP PN532 controller behind an ST7 USB microcontroller that presents it as a standard CCID smartcard reader. It is the default hardware assumption in a decade of NFC tutorials, libnfc documentation and MIFARE Classic write-ups, which is most of why it is still everywhere.
honest_take: Two things catch people out. First, it is 13.56 MHz only - it cannot see a 125 kHz HID Prox or EM4100 badge at all, and 'NFC reader' and 'RFID reader' get used interchangeably enough that people buy one expecting to clone a building badge. Second, ACS has formally end-of-lifed it while publicly warning about widespread counterfeits, so at US$35 you are buying an unknown clone whose firmware version and silicon you cannot verify, and clone-to-clone behaviour under libnfc genuinely varies - some only work through PC/SC, meaning they run on Windows and fail on Linux. What it is honestly good at is NFC Forum Type 1-4 NDEF read/write, and as the cheapest way to run the classic mfoc/mfcuk/libnfc MIFARE Classic workflow, with your PC doing all the computation. Past MIFARE Classic it runs out of road quickly: card emulation support through libnfc is poor, and the PN532 does not do ISO15693.
best_for: NDEF tag reading and writing - its genuine strength and why it is in every tutorial
The cheapest legitimate route into MIFARE Classic key recovery via mfoc / mfcuk
PC/SC and smartcard development where a standard CCID reader is what you want
not_for: 125 kHz badges of any kind - wrong frequency entirely
Card emulation - the PN532 has the mode, libnfc support is poor and the CCID wrapper gets in the way
ISO15693 / NFC Forum Type 5 tags
Anyone who needs to know what silicon they are actually running

hardware.mcu_primary_note: 8-bit low-power USB microcontroller with a smartcard interface, 16KB flash, 768 bytes RAM. Its only job is to bridge USB CCID to the PN532.

radios.note: NXP NFC controller: ISO14443A/MIFARE, ISO14443B, FeliCa and NFCIP-1. Reader/writer, card emulation and peer-to-peer modes in silicon. Does NOT implement ISO15693/NFC-V - that is a hardware limit, not a firmware one.

notable_physical: Multicolour status LED and a beeper - both of which are unavailable when driving the device through libnfc on Linux
Optional SAM slot on some variants

hf_1356_read.note: ISO14443A and B, MIFARE Classic / Ultralight / DESFire (identity and APDU layer), FeliCa, NFC Forum tag types 1-4. This is what the device is for.

hf_1356_write.note: NTAG and Ultralight writing is reliable. MIFARE Classic write support through libnfc is limited - some cards need manual formatting and some simply do not work. Widely reported, and it varies by clone.

hf_1356_emulate.note: The PN532 has a card-emulation mode, but libnfc's support for emulation and peer-to-peer on this device is documented as poor, and the CCID wrapper is in the way. Do not buy this to emulate a card - buy a Chameleon.

lf_125khz_read.note: Notable absence and the single most common purchasing mistake around this device. 13.56 MHz only. No HID Prox, no EM4100, no Indala, no Hitag.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: The whole mfoc / mfcuk / mfoc-hardnested workflow runs on this reader: nested (mfoc), darkside (mfcuk) and hardnested key recovery all work. Every part of the attack computation happens on your PC - the reader is a dumb RF front end passing frames. Slower and clumsier than a Proxmark, but it is the US$35 way in, and it is why this device appears in every MIFARE Classic tutorial written since about 2010.

mifare_desfire.note: Reads the UID and can carry ISO14443-4 APDUs to a DESFire, so you can enumerate applications and files. It cannot recover a DESFire AES key - no hardware can. Vendor spec sheets listing 'DESFire' mean 'can talk to one', not 'can clone one'.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: Full NFC Forum Type 1-4 NDEF read and write. This is the reader's real strength and the reason it is embedded in so much NDEF tooling. Worth restating what the column means: NDEF is a data format for records the tag hands to any reader that asks, so this is a formatting capability, not a security capability.

emv_read.note: As a PC/SC reader it carries EMV APDUs fine, and scripts in the RFIDIOt / nfcpy / pyResMan lineage will pull the PAN and expiry off many contactless bank cards, plus a transaction log on some issuers. IT CANNOT CLONE THE CARD OR MAKE A PAYMENT. Every transaction needs an Application Cryptogram computed inside the chip with an issuer key that never leaves it, and you cannot produce one. A dump of a card's static data is not a card. This is the single most misunderstood row in any NFC comparison table.

iso15693.note: The PN532 implements ISO14443A/B, FeliCa and NFCIP-1; ISO15693/NFC-V is not in its protocol set and the ACS firmware does not expose it. Some third-party spec tables list ISO15693 for this reader - we believe those are in error. If you need ISO15693, buy an ACR1252U/ACR1552U or a Proxmark. See research_gaps.

felica.note: PN532 supports FeliCa polling and libnfc exposes it - useful for reading IDm/PMm. FeliCa Standard's mutual authentication is not broken by this or anything else.

scriptable.note: libnfc, nfcpy, PC/SC bindings in every language, and a large body of existing example code. Ubiquity is the feature.

legal.notes: A commodity USB card reader sold openly on Amazon and used in payment, ticketing and access-control integration everywhere. Nothing about owning one is remarkable. The legal question attaches to what you read: pulling data off cards you do not own or are not authorised to read can engage computer-misuse or data-protection law, and reading strangers' bank cards in public is unlawful in most jurisdictions regardless of how little use the data is to you. Check your local law.

ecosystem.app_store: No - but an enormous body of libnfc/nfcpy/PC-SC example code targets it specifically

research_gaps: ISO15693 support is genuinely disputed in the sources. The nfc-tools device page lists ISO15693 among supported protocols; ACS's own datasheet historically lists NFC Forum Type 1-4 only (Type 5 = ISO15693 absent), and the PN532's documented protocol set does not include it. We could not read the PN532 datasheet directly in this session to settle it, so the 'no' above is a reasoned judgement, not a confirmed fact. Verify before relying on it.
Original release year could not be sourced; the product predates most of its own documentation.

Because ACS has EOL'd the product and warns of widespread counterfeits, no capability here can be guaranteed for a specific unit bought today - the silicon and firmware in a US$35 Amazon clone are unverifiable.
